claims.text: The Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al system is a lightweight refractory high-entropy alloy system.
Increasing Al content in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs increases chemical short-range ordering.
Increased chemical short-range ordering in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs produces a gradual increase in stacking-fault energy.
A lower-Al baseline should have lower SRO and lower stacking-fault energy than the higher-Al variants.
The low-Al baseline exhibits a moderate absolute level of SRO.
Increasing stacking-fault energy improves mechanical strength in this alloy system.
Elevated stacking-fault energy improves resistance to dislocation-motion-related weakening.
Al-induced SRO facilitates formation of a coherent, protective Al-rich surface oxide scale.
The protective Al-rich scale is likely Al2O3.
The Al-rich oxide scale reduces corrosion in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs.
The Al-rich oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation stability in Ti–V–Zr–Nb–Al HEAs.
Higher-Al variants should have higher yield strength than the low-Al baseline.
Increasing Al should preserve low density without a significant density increase.
Excessive Al can form brittle intermetallic phases that compromise mechanical integrity.
Trace additions or other alloying elements can suppress the beneficial SRO development.
Interactions with other elements may modify the effect of Al on the combined properties.

contradictions.description: The proposal says Al content will increase while all other elemental fractions or compositional parameters remain constant. Atomic fractions must sum to 100%, so increasing Al necessarily changes at least the normalized fractions of the other elements unless the intended control is that their mutual ratios remain constant.

Formation of detrimental brittle phases at excessive Al is defined as a condition under which the mechanism should cease to hold, but it is also declared to falsify the hypothesis. A result occurring outside a stated boundary normally does not falsify a hypothesis restricted by that boundary.
